subjects.name: English Language
subjects.blurb: Linguistic frameworks for analysing any text, and how children acquire language.

topics.title: Language Frameworks for Text Analysis
topics.summary: Lexis, grammar, phonology, pragmatics and discourse: the toolkit for analysing any text.

primer.heading: Why frameworks matter
primer.body: Examiners reward analysis that names a precise linguistic feature, gives an example from the text, and explains its effect in context: the writer's purpose, the audience and the genre. Feature-spotting without explaining effect scores poorly.

primer.heading: Lexis, semantics and grammar
primer.body: Lexis and semantics cover word choice and meaning: register, connotation, semantic fields, jargon. Grammar covers morphology (how words are built) and syntax (how sentences are built): sentence functions (declarative, interrogative, imperative, exclamative), sentence types (simple, compound, complex), modal verbs that show certainty or obligation, and active versus passive voice, which changes who is foregrounded.

primer.heading: Phonology, pragmatics and discourse
primer.body: Phonology covers sound: alliteration, rhythm, and in speech, prosodic features such as stress and intonation. Pragmatics covers meaning in context: implicature (what is implied), politeness strategies and deixis (words like "here", "now", "you" whose meaning depends on context). Discourse covers how a whole text is structured and how cohesion is created across it.

topics.title: Child Language Acquisition
topics.summary: The stages of early speech and the theories that try to explain them.

primer.heading: Stages
primer.body: Approximate ages vary between children. Babbling begins at around 6 months. The holophrastic (one-word) stage starts at about 12 months, where a single word can stand for a whole idea ("juice!"). The two-word stage follows at about 18 months ("daddy car"), then the telegraphic stage at about 24 months, where function words are dropped ("me want biscuit"), and then the post-telegraphic stage.

primer.heading: Theories
primer.body: Behaviourists such as Skinner argued children learn by imitation and reinforcement. Chomsky's nativist theory proposes an innate Language Acquisition Device, supported by the fact that children produce forms they have never heard. Piaget linked language to cognitive development. Interactionists such as Bruner (the Language Acquisition Support System) and Vygotsky (the zone of proximal development) stress the role of caregivers.

primer.heading: Virtuous errors
primer.body: Overgeneralisation errors such as "I goed" or "two mouses" are called virtuous errors: the child has learnt a rule (add -ed for past tense, -s for plural) and applies it too widely. Because adults do not say "goed", these errors are evidence against pure imitation. Berko's "wug" test showed children apply plural rules to invented words.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.blurb: Pure mathematics: the calculus at the centre of AS and A Level.

topics.title: Differentiation Techniques
topics.summary: Standard derivatives, the chain, product and quotient rules, and stationary points.

primer.heading: Standard derivatives
primer.body: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹. d/dx(eᵏˣ) = keᵏˣ. d/dx(ln x) = 1/x. With x in radians: d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(cos x) = −sin x, d/dx(tan x) = sec²x.

primer.heading: Chain rule
primer.body: For a function of a function, y = f(g(x)), dy/dx = f′(g(x)) × g′(x): differentiate the outside, keep the inside, multiply by the derivative of the inside. For y = (3x² + 2)⁵, dy/dx = 5(3x² + 2)⁴ × 6x = 30x(3x² + 2)⁴.

primer.heading: Product and quotient rules
primer.body: For y = uv, dy/dx = u(dv/dx) + v(du/dx). For y = u/v, dy/dx = (v(du/dx) − u(dv/dx)) / v². Identify u and v first and write down du/dx and dv/dx before substituting.

primer.heading: Stationary points
primer.body: Solve dy/dx = 0. Classify with the second derivative: d²y/dx² > 0 gives a minimum, d²y/dx² < 0 a maximum. If it equals 0, test the gradient on either side.

terms: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx for composite functions.

topics.title: Integration
topics.summary: Integration as the reverse of differentiation, standard integrals, definite integrals and area.

primer.heading: Reverse of differentiation
primer.body: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c for n ≠ −1. ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + c. Always include the constant of integration in an indefinite integral; examiners deduct marks when it is missing.

primer.heading: Standard integrals
primer.body: ∫eᵏˣ dx = (1/k)eᵏˣ + c. ∫cos kx dx = (1/k) sin kx + c. ∫sin kx dx = −(1/k) cos kx + c. Check by differentiating your answer.

primer.heading: Definite integrals and area
primer.body: A definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) has no constant. It gives the area between the curve and the x-axis when the curve is above the axis. Where the curve is below the axis the integral is negative, so split the interval at the roots and add the absolute values.

topics.title: Kinematics and Projectiles
topics.summary: The equations of uniformly accelerated motion, free fall and projectile motion.

primer.heading: The suvat equations
primer.body: For constant acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t. List the three quantities you know and the one you want, then pick the equation that contains exactly those four.

primer.heading: Free fall
primer.body: Near the Earth's surface, ignoring air resistance, every object accelerates downwards at g = 9.81 m s⁻². Choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent: with up as positive, a = −9.81 m s⁻².

primer.heading: Projectiles
primer.body: Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately; they share only the time of flight. Horizontally there is no force (ignoring air resistance), so velocity is constant. Vertically the motion is free fall. For a launch at angle θ with speed u, the components are u cos θ horizontally and u sin θ vertically.

topics.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.summary: The defining equation a = −ω²x, its solutions, energy in SHM, and springs and pendulums.

primer.heading: Definition
primer.body: Motion is simple harmonic when the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and always directed towards that point: a = −ω²x, where ω = 2πf = 2π/T is the angular frequency.

primer.heading: Solutions and maximum values
primer.body: If timing starts at maximum displacement, x = A cos ωt. Velocity v = ±ω√(A² − x²), so the maximum speed is ωA, at the equilibrium position. The maximum acceleration is ω²A, at the extremes of the motion.

primer.heading: Springs, pendulums and energy
primer.body: A mass on a spring has T = 2π√(m/k). A simple pendulum, for small angles, has T = 2π√(l/g), independent of the mass and of the amplitude. In undamped SHM total energy is constant: kinetic energy is greatest at equilibrium and potential energy greatest at maximum displacement.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.blurb: Physical chemistry: energy changes and how fast reactions go.

topics.title: Chemical Energetics
topics.summary: Enthalpy changes, calorimetry, Hess's law and bond enthalpies.

primer.heading: Enthalpy change
primer.body: ΔH is the heat energy change at constant pressure. Exothermic reactions have negative ΔH; endothermic reactions have positive ΔH. Standard conditions are 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K. Standard enthalpy of formation is for forming 1 mol of a compound from its elements in their standard states; standard enthalpy of combustion is for burning 1 mol completely in oxygen.

primer.heading: Calorimetry
primer.body: Heat transferred q = mcΔT, using the mass of the solution (1 cm³ ≈ 1 g) and c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Then ΔH = −q / n, where n is the moles of the limiting reactant. The sign is negative if the temperature rose.

primer.heading: Hess's law and bond enthalpies
primer.body: Hess's law: the enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken. Build a cycle through formation or combustion data. With bond enthalpies, ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Bond enthalpies are averages over many compounds, so results differ slightly from experimental data.

topics.title: Reaction Kinetics
topics.summary: Rate equations, orders of reaction, half-life and the rate-determining step.

primer.heading: Rate equations
primer.body: For A + B → products, rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, where m and n are the orders with respect to each reactant and m + n is the overall order. Orders are found by experiment, not from the balanced equation. If doubling [A] doubles the rate, the order in A is 1; if it quadruples the rate, the order is 2; if the rate is unchanged, the order is 0.

primer.heading: Units and half-life
primer.body: The units of k depend on the overall order: s⁻¹ for first order, mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹ for second order, mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹ for third order. A first-order reaction has a constant half-life, independent of concentration, and k = ln 2 / t½.

primer.heading: Mechanisms and temperature
primer.body: The rate-determining step is the slowest step in a mechanism. Species in the rate equation appear in or before that step; a reactant with order zero is not involved until after it. Raising temperature increases k because a larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy, as shown by the Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(−Ea/RT).

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.blurb: Biological molecules, enzymes and the flow of genetic information.

topics.title: Enzymes
topics.summary: How enzymes work, the factors affecting their rate, and inhibition.

primer.heading: How enzymes work
primer.body: Enzymes are globular proteins that act as biological catalysts by lowering the activation energy of a reaction. The substrate binds to the active site, which has a specific tertiary structure, to form an enzyme–substrate complex. In the induced-fit model the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, putting strain on bonds.

primer.heading: Factors affecting rate
primer.body: Rising temperature increases kinetic energy and collisions until the optimum; above it, hydrogen and ionic bonds in the enzyme break, the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured. pH away from the optimum alters charges in the active site. Increasing substrate concentration raises the rate until all active sites are occupied and the rate reaches Vmax.

primer.heading: Inhibition
primer.body: A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate and binds to the active site; its effect can be overcome by raising substrate concentration, so Vmax is unchanged but more substrate is needed to reach it. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere (an allosteric site), changing the shape of the active site; adding more substrate does not overcome it, so Vmax falls.

topics.title: DNA Replication and Protein Synthesis

primer.heading: Semi-conservative replication
primer.body: DNA helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases. Each strand acts as a template; free nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A–T, C–G) and DNA polymerase joins them with phosphodiester bonds, working in the 5′ to 3′ direction. The lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase. Each new molecule has one original and one new strand, as Meselson and Stahl showed using ¹⁵N and ¹⁴N.

primer.heading: Transcription
primer.body: In the nucleus, RNA polymerase builds an mRNA copy of a gene using one DNA strand as the template, with uracil in place of thymine. In eukaryotes the pre-mRNA is spliced to remove introns before the mRNA leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore.

primer.heading: Translation
primer.body: At a ribosome, each mRNA codon (a triplet of bases) is matched by the complementary anticodon of a tRNA carrying a specific amino acid. Peptide bonds form between adjacent amino acids. The genetic code is degenerate (most amino acids have more than one codon), non-overlapping and universal.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.blurb: Physical systems: drainage basins and coastal landscapes.

topics.title: Hydrology: Drainage Basins and Storm Hydrographs
topics.summary: The drainage basin as an open system, the water balance, and what controls a storm hydrograph.

primer.heading: The drainage basin system
primer.body: A drainage basin is an open system. Inputs: precipitation. Stores: interception, surface storage, soil water, groundwater and the channel. Flows: throughfall, stemflow, infiltration, overland flow, throughflow, percolation and groundwater flow. Outputs: evapotranspiration and channel discharge. The water balance is P = Q + E ± ΔS.

primer.heading: Reading a storm hydrograph
primer.body: A storm hydrograph plots discharge (m³ s⁻¹) against time after a rainfall event. Lag time is the time between peak rainfall and peak discharge. The rising limb shows discharge increasing; the falling (recession) limb shows it returning towards baseflow, the slow contribution of groundwater.

primer.heading: What makes a "flashy" hydrograph
primer.body: A short lag time and high peak result from impermeable rock or saturated soil, steep slopes, a circular basin with high drainage density, little vegetation and urbanisation, which adds impermeable surfaces and drains. Permeable rock, forest cover and an elongated basin lengthen the lag time and lower the peak.

topics.title: Coastal Systems and Landscapes
topics.summary: Waves, sediment movement, erosional and depositional landforms, and coastal management.

primer.heading: Waves
primer.body: Constructive waves are low, with a long wavelength and low frequency (about 6–8 per minute); the swash is stronger than the backwash, so they build beaches. Destructive waves are high and steep with a higher frequency (about 10–14 per minute); the backwash is stronger, so they remove material.

primer.heading: Erosional landforms
primer.body: Where rock types alternate along a discordant coastline, softer rock erodes into bays and harder rock is left as headlands. Wave refraction concentrates energy on headlands, where a crack can enlarge into a cave, then an arch, a stack and finally a stump. Cliff retreat leaves a wave-cut platform at its base.

primer.heading: Deposition and management
primer.body: Longshore drift moves sediment along the coast in the direction of the prevailing wind: swash moves up the beach at an angle, backwash returns straight down. Where the coastline changes direction, deposition can build a spit. Shoreline Management Plans divide coasts into sediment cells and choose a policy: hold the line, advance the line, managed realignment or no active intervention.

Movement of sediment along the coast by waves.
